blocks.text: Rate limiting, account lockout and CAPTCHA protect login, reset, verification, search and expensive API endpoints from brute force, enumeration and abuse. They are weak when the limit key is attacker-controlled (client IP headers, account identifier spelling), when the same action is reachable through several routes, or when the counter resets unexpectedly. This category lists the variations used to test whether the limit really holds.

items: Client-IP headers trusted for the limit key (`X-Forwarded-For` and similar)
Endpoint aliases: path case, trailing characters, encodings and API versions that map to the same handler but a different counter
Parameter noise and account-identifier variants: email case, plus-addressing, whitespace and Unicode forms
Counter resets by a successful login, a password change or a new session
Batching inside one request: GraphQL aliases, JSON arrays, multi-part bodies
Concurrent requests that all pass the check before the counter increments
CAPTCHA parameters that can be omitted, reused, replayed or set to a fixed value; a CAPTCHA enforced on the web form but not on the API
Limits applied per node and not globally

blocks.text: Establish the baseline: how many failed attempts are accepted, what the block response looks like, and how long it lasts. Then change one variable at a time (header, path, case, method, content type) and see whether the counter restarts. Use test accounts and a small cap; the goal is to show that the limit can be evaded, not to attack real accounts or exhaust a service. For CAPTCHA, test removal, reuse, empty and stale tokens, and whether an alternative client or endpoint skips it.
See `rate-limit-bypass-payloads.txt` for header, path, identifier, batching and CAPTCHA tests. Replace example hosts and parameter names with the target's.

sections.label: Rate-Limit, Brute-Force and CAPTCHA Bypass Payloads
Client-IP header rotation (change the value on each request)
Endpoint aliases that may map to the same handler with a separate counter
Parameter noise (each request looks different to a naive key)
Account identifier variants that may keep separate counters but map to one account
JSON and GraphQL batching (many attempts in one request)
Header and session variations (a new identity for the limiter)
Concurrency checks (see Race-Conditions): send many attempts in parallel before the counter increments
CAPTCHA bypass: parameter tests (submit with these in place of a valid token)
Resource-based limit tests on non-login endpoints

# Counter-reset checks (sequence descriptions)
# Make N-1 wrong attempts, log in successfully to your own other account, then make more wrong attempts and see whether the counter was cleared
# Make N-1 wrong attempts, request a password reset or resend, then continue
# Make N-1 wrong attempts, open a new session or restart the flow, then continue
# Wait for the stated lockout period and check that the next failure restarts the lockout
# Check whether lockout is per account (denial-of-service risk for the owner) or per source

# Concurrency checks (see Race-Conditions): send many attempts in parallel before the counter increments
# seq 1 50 | xargs -P 25 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST https://app.example.test/login -d "user=test&pass=wrong{}"

# Compare IPv4 and IPv6 behaviour

# Omit the CAPTCHA parameter entirely
# Replay a previously valid token on a second request and a later session
